ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: This is a house floor plan, the bottom is an entire terrace labeled “Terrasse”, above it is divided into three rooms 1, 2, 3, the lower left is 4, and the lower right is 5. The doorways in the figure are represented by short diagonal lines, so each door can be regarded as an edge of the graph. Then reason: The door connections readable from the figure are Terrasse-4, 4-1, 1-2, 2-3, 2-5, 3-5. Thus the degree of each point is: the degree of Terrasse is 1, the degree of room 4 is 2, the degree of room 1 is 2, the degree of room 2 is 3, the degree of room 3 is 2, and the degree of room 5 is 2. Renate wants “to pass through every door exactly once”, this is an Euler path. The start point and end point of an Euler path are exactly the two odd-degree vertices. She starts from Terrasse, and the other odd-degree vertex is room 2, so she will finally end in room 2.

raw_record.question_text: The diagram shows the floor plan of Renate's house. Renate enters her house from the terrace (Terrasse) and walks through every door of the house exactly once. Which room does she end up in?

method.method_draft: First read the floor-plan image as a graph: vertices are Terrasse and rooms 1, 2, 3, 4, 5; each visible door gap is an edge. From the image, the door adjacencies are Terrasse-4, 4-1, 1-2, 2-3, 2-5, and 3-5. Then use the text condition that Renate starts at Terrasse and crosses every door exactly once, i.e. she makes an Euler trail starting at Terrasse. Count incident doors: Terrasse has degree 1, room 4 has degree 2, room 1 has degree 2, room 2 has degree 3, room 3 has degree 2, and room 5 has degree 2. In an Euler trail, the endpoints are exactly the odd-degree vertices. Since one odd vertex is the starting Terrasse, the other odd vertex is room 2, so she ends in room 2.

method.method_draft: First describe the image structure: the terrace has only one visible door into room 4; room 4 connects upward to room 1; room 1 connects to room 2; room 2 connects to rooms 1, 3, and 5; room 3 connects to rooms 2 and 5; room 5 connects to rooms 2 and 3. The remaining unused doors form the small cycle between rooms 2, 3, and 5: use either 2 -> 3 -> 5 -> 2 or 2 -> 5 -> 3 -> 2. In both cases every listed door is used exactly once and the final room is 2.
